references.text: Jesus uses the same image of the lamp in the Sermon on the Mount: no one lights a lamp and puts it under a bowl, but on a lampstand, so that it gives light to all in the house.
Mark's parallel to this saying, where Jesus asks whether a lamp is brought in to be put under a bowl or under a bed, and not on a lampstand.

Luke repeats this image later in another context, where Jesus says that no one lights a lamp and puts it in the cellar or under a bowl, but on a lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light.
The path of the righteous is like the shining light that grows brighter and brighter until it is full daylight – a parallel to the idea that the light should shine openly and not be hidden.
Isaiah urges us to let the light shine, for the Lord's glory rises over his people – thematically parallel to the idea that the light should not be hidden but set forth.
Jesus calls his disciples the light of the world – a city on a hill cannot be hidden. This provides the broader context for the lamp metaphor that the light of faith should be visible.
Paul urges believers to shine as lights in the world and hold out the word of life – a practical application of the principle that the light should not be hidden.
Peter refers to the prophetic word as a lamp shining in a dark place, which connects to the image of the lamp meant to give light to those in the room.
